html:
The Council for Mutual Economic Assistance, or Comecon, was the trade bloc of the Soviet Union and the communist states of the Eastern bloc, from 1949 to 1991.

Stalin set it up in January 1949, partly in answer to the American Marshall Plan, which he had forbidden Eastern Europe to join. The founders were the Soviet Union, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria. East Germany joined in 1950, and later members outside Europe were Mongolia, Cuba and Vietnam.

In theory it coordinated the planned economies so each country could specialise. In practice trade was mostly between each member and the Soviet Union, set by bargaining between states instead of markets. The Soviet Union supplied oil and gas at low prices, through pipelines such as Druzhba, "friendship", and took machines, buses, food and consumer goods in return.

It never matched the Western European common market set up by the Treaty of Rome. After the revolutions of 1989 its members turned west, and Comecon was dissolved in June 1991, months before the Soviet Union itself.
sum: The Council for Mutual Economic Assistance, or Comecon, was the trade bloc of the Soviet Union and the communist states of the Eastern bloc, from 1949 to 1991.
